name: Fluent Boards
notes: Two boards. Website: where the team and clients put requests and feedback. Work moves from To-Do to In Progress, then to Done (please check) so the person who asked can confirm, and only then to Closed. Website Setup: the accounts and keys the site needs, one task each, in the order to do them, with plain steps and links anyone can follow. Never paste a password or key into a task or comment: each task says where the key belongs. Other plugins add their own setup tasks to the same board (SEO Pro Directory adds Google Maps Platform and Outscraper). Add more boards the same way: one per area of work, with a check step before Closed.

fluentboards_boards.title: Website
fluentboards_boards.description: Plans, requests and feedback on the website's design, features and user experience.

fluentboards_boards.title: Website Setup
fluentboards_boards.description: The accounts and keys this site needs, in the order to set them up. Each task has the steps and links. Never paste a password or key into a task or comment.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Accounts and Keys Checklist
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Every account this site needs, and the task on this board that sets it up. Open each account in the business's name, with an email address the business keeps, and turn on two-factor authentication. Keys go where each task says (the plugin's settings, `wp-config.php` or the aidevops secret store), never into a task or comment.

- **Hosting:** Hostinger (Setup Hosting), with SSH for your AI assistant (Setup SSH Access for aidevops).
- **Domain and DNS:** a domain registrar and Cloudflare (Setup Cloudflare). The same Cloudflare account gives the cache token (Clear Cloudflare's cache with LiteSpeed Cache), Turnstile spam protection for forms and logins, and R2 file storage.
- **Email:** mailboxes people write to, such as hello@ and support@ (Setup Business Email), and Amazon SES for the emails the site sends (Setup Email Sending).
- **Google:** one Google account for the business, with a Google Cloud project and billing (Setup Google Cloud) for the Google APIs the site uses, such as Cloud Translation on a site in more than one language; and Search Console (Setup Google Search Console).
- **Bing:** Bing Webmaster Tools, signed in with that Google account or a Microsoft account the business keeps (Setup Bing Webmaster Tools).
- **Payments:** Stripe, PayPal, Paddle or Polar (Setup Payment Processing).
- **Other plugins** add tasks for their own accounts to this board, such as SEO Pro Directory's Google Maps Platform and Outscraper.

**A site copied from another one** (a template, a demo or a review copy) arrives with that site's keys. They belong to its owner: they bill that owner and stop working when the owner changes them. Check each place below and put in your own key, or remove what the site does not use:

- **FluentSMTP → Settings:** email connections (Amazon SES keys).
- **LiteSpeed Cache → CDN → Cloudflare:** the API token.
- **Settings → Cloudflare Turnstile:** the site key and secret key.
- **Settings → TranslatePress → Automatic Translation:** the Google Translate API key.
- **The payment plugin's settings:** API keys and webhook secrets.
- **`wp-config.php`:** keys defined for plugins. Your AI can list their names, never their values, with `wp config list --fields=name`.

Done when every account the site uses is in the business's name and every key on the site is its own.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Hosting (Hostinger)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Where the website lives. We use Hostinger: fast LiteSpeed servers, daily backups and SSH access for your AI assistant.

1. Open [Hostinger](https://hostinger.com?REFERRALCODE=1MARCUS454) and choose a **Premium** or **Business** web hosting plan, or Cloud hosting for bigger sites. The Single plan has no SSH access, which aidevops needs.
2. Sign up, pay, and turn on two-factor authentication in your account settings.
3. In hPanel, add the website and its domain (a temporary domain is fine until the domain is ready).
4. Choose the newest PHP version: in hPanel, open the website's **Advanced → PHP Configuration** and pick the highest version listed. Newer PHP is faster and gets security fixes for longer. Update WordPress first, as each release lists the PHP versions it supports. If a plugin the site needs does not support the newest PHP yet (its page lists the PHP versions it supports), pick the newest one it does, and add a card to move up later. Check afterwards that the home page and wp-admin load; if either shows an error, choose the previous version again in the same place. **Tools → Site Health → Info → Server** shows the version the site runs.
5. Note the plan name and data centre in a comment on this task, never a password.

Done when the site loads at its address on the newest PHP version it supports and you can log in to hPanel.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Cloudflare (domain DNS and security)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Cloudflare runs the domain's DNS for free and protects and speeds up the site.

1. Buy the domain if you have not yet, at any registrar (such as [101domain](https://www.101domain.com/affiliate/evergreenje.html)) or Cloudflare itself.
2. [Create a Cloudflare account](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/account/create-account/) and turn on two-factor authentication.
3. Add the domain ([full setup](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/zone-setups/full-setup/setup/)): Cloudflare copies the existing DNS records. Check the website's A record points at your hosting's IP (hPanel shows it).
4. At your registrar, replace the nameservers with the two Cloudflare gives you. It can take up to a day.
5. SSL/TLS: choose [Full (strict)](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/origin-configuration/ssl-modes/full-strict/) once the host has an SSL certificate.

Done when Cloudflare shows the domain as **Active** and the site loads over https.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Protect the Site from Scanners (Cloudflare security rules)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Scanners try every website for leaked password and settings files, such as `/.env`, `/.git` or a `.sql` backup, and can send thousands of requests in a few minutes. WordPress answers each one with a "not found" page it builds from the database, so a busy scanner uses up the hosting plan's CPU and database connections and slows the site or stops it (hPanel shows the plan's resource limits reached). Two free Cloudflare rules stop them before they reach the server.

1. In Cloudflare, open the domain, then **Security → Security rules** (older dashboards: **Security → WAF**) and create a **Custom rule**. Name it `Block scanner probes`, choose **Edit expression**, paste this, set the action to **Block** and deploy it: `(http.request.uri.path contains "/.env" or http.request.uri.path contains "/.git/" or ends_with(http.request.uri.path, "/.git") or http.request.uri.path contains "/.aws/" or http.request.uri.path contains "/.ssh/" or http.request.uri.path contains "/.svn/" or http.request.uri.path contains "/.dev.vars" or http.request.uri.path contains "/.htpasswd" or http.request.uri.path contains "/.DS_Store" or http.request.uri.path contains "docker-compose" or http.request.uri.path contains "/phpinfo" or http.request.uri.path contains "wp-config.php." or http.request.uri.path contains "/vendor/phpunit/" or ends_with(http.request.uri.path, ".sql") or ends_with(http.request.uri.path, ".sql.gz"))`
2. On the same page, create a **Rate limiting rule** named `Limit requests per visitor`, with this expression, so pictures, styles and scripts do not count: `(not http.request.uri.path.extension in {"js" "css" "png" "jpg" "jpeg" "gif" "svg" "webp" "avif" "ico" "woff" "woff2" "ttf" "map"})`. Count requests by **IP**; when they exceed **100** in **10 seconds**, **Block** for **10 seconds**. A person never opens that many pages so fast, and a scanner is stopped within seconds. The Free plan allows one rate limiting rule per domain.
3. **Other services on the domain** (such as Nextcloud, a mail app or a file app on a subdomain): put `http.host in {"example.com" "www.example.com"} and ` (the website's own addresses) straight after the first bracket of both expressions, so those services are not affected.
4. **A multisite network** (such as Ultimate Multisite with sites at subdomains): the rules cover every site at the domain. Keep the wildcard DNS record (`*`) when new sites get their own subdomain, as they need it. Each mapped domain (a site with its own domain) is a separate domain in Cloudflare: add both rules there too.
5. Leave **Bot Fight Mode** off: it challenges requests that do not come from a browser, such as plugin licence checks, uptime monitors and your AI assistant. Blocking AI crawlers is a separate choice, as they also bring the site into AI answers.
6. Test: open `https://<domain>/.env`. Cloudflare's "Sorry, you have been blocked" page shows. Check that the home page, wp-admin and a form work as before.

**With aidevops:** it can add both rules through Cloudflare's API with your Cloudflare access from its secret store, test them, and a day later check **Security → Events** for real visitors blocked by mistake.

Done when `/.env` shows Cloudflare's block page, the home page and wp-admin load, and a day later Security → Events shows no real visitors blocked.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Clear Cloudflare's cache with LiteSpeed Cache
fluentboards_tasks.description:
LiteSpeed Cache keeps fast copies of pages on the server, and Cloudflare can keep its own. When LiteSpeed Cache empties its copies (Purge All, after updates), Cloudflare's stay until they expire, so visitors can see old pages. With a Cloudflare token, every Purge All empties Cloudflare too.

1. In Cloudflare, open **My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token → Create Custom Token** ([Cloudflare's guide to creating a token](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/)). Name it after the site. Permissions: **Zone → Cache Purge → Purge** and **Zone → Zone → Read** (LiteSpeed Cache looks the zone up with it). Zone Resources: **Include → Specific zone →** this site's domain. Create it and copy the token: Cloudflare shows it only once.
2. In WordPress, open **LiteSpeed Cache → CDN → Cloudflare** ([LiteSpeed's CDN settings guide](https://docs.litespeedtech.com/lscache/lscwp/cdn/)). Turn **Cloudflare API** on, paste the token as the API token, leave the email empty, enter the domain, turn **Clear Cloudflare cache** on and save.
3. Test with **Purge All** (LiteSpeed Cache in the admin bar or Toolbox): it says Cloudflare was notified.

**Clear Cloudflare cache** empties the whole domain on Cloudflare. If other websites share this domain (on subdomains), leave it off and turn on **SEO Pro Stack → Speed → Clear Cloudflare's copies of pages** instead: it empties only this site's address, after a Purge All and after a post is published or updated, and uses LiteSpeed Cache's token. Never paste the token into a task or comment.

**With aidevops over SSH:** it can create the token through Cloudflare's API with your Cloudflare access from its secret store, then save it with WP-CLI without showing it. Test with `wp litespeed-purge all`. On a multisite network, use `wp litespeed-purge blog <id> --url=<site address>` instead: `all` empties every site's cache on the network, and without `--url` the main site's Cloudflare settings are used.

Done when Purge All reports that Cloudflare was notified. (Only if the site's pages are cached by Cloudflare, `cf-cache-status` on the home page shows `MISS` straight after a purge; a visitor's request can refill it first, and `DYNAMIC` is normal when Cloudflare does not cache HTML.)

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Spam Protection (Cloudflare Turnstile)
fluentboards_tasks.after: Clear Cloudflare's cache with LiteSpeed Cache
fluentboards_tasks.description:
[Cloudflare Turnstile](https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/) stops spam bots on the site's forms, login and registration, usually without a puzzle for people. It is free, in the same Cloudflare account as the domain. The Simple Cloudflare Turnstile plugin adds it to the site.

1. In Cloudflare, open **Turnstile → Add widget**. Name it after the site, add the site's domain as a hostname (on a multisite, each domain its sites use), choose the **Managed** mode and create it.
2. Copy the **Site Key** and **Secret Key** it shows.
3. In WordPress, open **Settings → Cloudflare Turnstile**, paste both keys and save. Complete the test response it then shows: Turnstile is added to no form until that test succeeds. On a multisite, do this on each site.
4. Choose where it shows: **Login Form**, **Register Form**, the password reset and comments, the forms plugin (such as **Enable on all Fluent Forms**) and, on a shop, WooCommerce's forms.
5. Log out and in again, and send a test from one form.

A site copied from another one has that site's keys here: replace them with your own, or the check fails on your domain. Never paste a key into a task or comment. Done when the test response succeeds and a form sends with Turnstile showing.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup aidevops (your AI assistant)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
[aidevops](https://aidevops.sh) lets an AI assistant on your computer set up and look after this site with you: plugin updates, settings, checks and fixes, and these setup tasks.

1. On a Mac, open Terminal and run `brew install marcusquinn/tap/aidevops && aidevops update`. On Linux or Windows (WSL): `npm install -g aidevops && aidevops update`.
2. Follow the setup it starts. Check with `aidevops status`.
3. Start a session with `aidevops opencode` and type `/onboarding` for a guided tour.
4. Keys go in its secret store, never in chat: `aidevops secret set NAME` asks for the value privately.

Docs: [aidevops.sh/docs](https://aidevops.sh/docs) and [GitHub](https://github.com/marcusquinn/aidevops).

Done when `aidevops status` shows it ready.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup SSH Access for aidevops
fluentboards_tasks.description:
SSH lets aidevops run WordPress's command line (WP-CLI) on the server, so your AI can do in seconds what takes many clicks, and check its own work. Recommended for every site.

1. On your computer, make a key if you have none: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` (press Enter for the defaults; a passphrase is optional).
2. In Hostinger's hPanel, open **Advanced → SSH Access**, turn SSH on and add your public key (the text in `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`). Hostinger's guide: [connect via SSH](https://www.hostinger.com/support/1583245-how-to-connect-to-a-hosting-plan-via-ssh-in-hostinger/).
3. Note the IP, port and username hPanel shows, and ask your AI to add a short name for the server to `~/.ssh/config` and test it with `ssh <name> 'wp --info'`.
4. Tell aidevops which folder the site is in (hPanel shows it, such as `domains/example.com/public_html`).

**If `wp --info` ends with an error about `proc_open()`:** over SSH, PHP is the account's default version, which can differ from the website's, and Hostinger turns `proc_open()` off for some PHP versions on some plans. Most WP-CLI commands still work, but `wp --info` and the `wp db` commands need it. Ask your AI to find a PHP version that has it, with `for v in 82 83 84 85; do echo "$v $(/opt/alt/php$v/usr/bin/php -r 'var_dump(function_exists("proc_open"));')"; done`, and run WP-CLI with the newest version that has it (the site's own PHP version or close to it, so the site's plugins load), for example `/opt/alt/php84/usr/bin/php /usr/local/bin/wp --info`, then `/opt/alt/php84/usr/bin/php /usr/local/bin/wp option get home` from the site's folder, which loads the site. This changes nothing for the website, which keeps the PHP version chosen in Setup Hosting.

Never share your hosting password or private key. Done when `wp --info` works over SSH, with the default PHP or the one your AI found.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Connect your AI to this Board
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Optional. With SSH (the task before), aidevops can already read and update this board through WP-CLI. To let another AI client (ChatGPT, Claude) work on the board directly:

1. In Fluent Boards, open **Settings → MCP for AI Agents** (Fluent Boards 2.2 or later) and turn **Enable MCP for AI Agents** on. If it asks for the MCP adapter, install it from that screen.
2. Follow **Connect your AI client** there: it makes a key (a WordPress application password) for your user and shows the address to give your AI client. On a multisite, Fluent Boards must be network-activated first.
3. Leave **Allow board members to use MCP** off unless the whole team needs it.

Without any AI: work through the tasks in order and move each to Done when finished.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Business Email (Purelymail)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Mailboxes people write to, such as hello@ and support@ at your domain. [Purelymail](https://purelymail.com/) is simple and low-cost ([pricing](https://purelymail.com/pricing)).

1. Sign up and add your domain.
2. Purelymail lists DNS records (MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC): add each in Cloudflare → DNS, with the proxy (orange cloud) off. A domain has one SPF record: if another service asks for one, merge them into it.
3. Create the mailboxes, or one mailbox with aliases, and add them to your email app. Purelymail's [docs](https://purelymail.com/docs/) cover each step.
4. Send a test to and from an outside address.

Done when mail arrives both ways and Purelymail shows the DNS records as correct.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Email Sending (Amazon SES)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
The website's own emails (forms, newsletters, password resets) go through [Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/), so they reach inboxes instead of spam. FluentSMTP connects WordPress to it.

1. Create an AWS account, turn on two-factor authentication, and open [SES](https://console.aws.amazon.com/ses/) in the region nearest your visitors.
2. [Verify your domain](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/creating-identities.html): add the three DKIM CNAME records in Cloudflare → DNS (proxy off), and a DMARC record if Purelymail did not add one ([DMARC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-email-authentication-dmarc.html)).
3. [Request production access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/request-production-access.html), saying the site sends only emails people ask for.
4. Create access keys that may only send email, and enter them in **FluentSMTP → Settings** ([guide](https://fluentsmtp.com/docs/set-up-amazon-ses-in-fluent-smtp/)), then send a test.

FluentSMTP encrypts the key with the site's salts: re-enter it if they change. A site copied from another one has that site's connections in FluentSMTP: delete them once yours works. Done when the test email arrives.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup File Storage (Cloudflare R2)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
[Cloudflare R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/get-started/) stores files off the server, such as backups, with no download fees. The free allowance covers most sites.

1. In Cloudflare, open **R2 Object Storage** and add a payment method (needed even for the free tier).
2. Create a bucket named after the site, such as `example-com-backups`.
3. [Create an API token](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/tokens/) with **Object Read & Write** for that bucket only.
4. Give the access key, secret and endpoint to the plugin that uses them (your backup plugin), or to aidevops with `aidevops secret set`. Never in a task or comment.

Done when a first backup appears in the bucket.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Google Cloud
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Google services the site uses (such as Maps, or Cloud Translation on a site in more than one language) are billed through a Google Cloud project. Search Console, which is free, has its own task.

1. Sign in to the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com/) with the business's Google account.
2. Create a billing account (a card is needed; most small sites stay in the free monthly credit), then a project named after the site.
3. Set a [budget alert](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets), such as 20 a month in your currency. It emails you as spending nears the amount but does not stop it: when one arrives, check what is using the API and lower or turn off what you do not need. To set a hard limit, [cap each API's daily requests](https://cloud.google.com/apis/docs/capping-api-usage).

Done when the project exists with billing and a budget alert.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Google Search Console
fluentboards_tasks.description:
[Search Console](https://search.google.com/search-console/about) shows how Google sees the site: the searches it appears in, the pages Google cannot index and why, and problems to fix. It is free, and separate from Google Cloud. Do it once the site is on its own domain and open to search engines (**Settings → Reading**).

1. Sign in to Search Console with the business's Google account and add a **Domain** property for the site's domain.
2. Google shows a TXT record: add it in Cloudflare → DNS, then click **Verify** (it can take a few minutes).
3. Open **Sitemaps** and submit the site's sitemap address (with Rank Math, `sitemap_index.xml`).
4. Give the team access under **Settings → Users and permissions**, rather than sharing a login.

Bing has its own task, next. Done when the property is verified and the sitemap shows **Success**.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Bing Webmaster Tools
fluentboards_tasks.description:
[Bing Webmaster Tools](https://www.bing.com/webmasters/about) does for Bing what Search Console does for Google: the searches the site appears in, the pages Bing cannot index and why, and a place to submit the sitemap. Bing's results also appear in other search engines, such as DuckDuckGo, Yahoo and Ecosia, and in Microsoft Copilot. It is free. Do it after Setup Google Search Console, once the site is on its own domain and open to search engines (**Settings → Reading**).

1. Open Bing Webmaster Tools and sign in with the business's Google account (or a Microsoft account the business keeps).
2. Choose **Import your sites from GSC** and allow it to read Search Console: it adds the site, already verified, with the sitemaps submitted there. Without Search Console, choose **Add your site manually**, enter the site's address and verify it with the **CNAME** record Bing shows, added in Cloudflare → DNS with the proxy (orange cloud) off.
3. Open **Sitemaps**. If the sitemap is not listed, choose **Submit sitemap** and enter its full address (with Rank Math, `https://<domain>/sitemap_index.xml`).
4. Give the team access under **User management** (in Settings), rather than sharing a login.

Optional, with Rank Math: turn on its **Instant Indexing** module, which tells Bing at once when a page is published or changed (IndexNow). Done when the site shows as verified and the sitemap's status is **Success**.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Google Translation (Cloud Translation API)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
TranslatePress translates the site's pages into its other languages automatically, with Google's Cloud Translation API, billed to the Google Cloud project from **Setup Google Cloud**. Google gives a free allowance each month; after it, you pay by the number of characters translated.

1. In the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com/), in the site's project, open **APIs & Services → Library**, find **Cloud Translation API** and click **Enable**.
2. Open **APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → API key** ([Google's guide to API keys](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/api-keys)).
3. Restrict the key. **API restrictions:** Cloud Translation API only. **Application restrictions:** Websites, with the address TranslatePress shows as **Your HTTP referrer is** under its Google key (TranslatePress sends it with each request).
4. In WordPress, open **Settings → TranslatePress → Automatic Translation**, turn on **Enable Automatic Translation**, choose **Google Translate v2**, paste the key as the **Google Translate API Key** and save. Set **Limit machine translation / characters per day** so one busy day cannot run up the bill.
5. Open a page in another language that was not translated before: it shows translated.

A site copied from another one has that site's key here: replace it with yours. Never paste the key into a task or comment. Done when a new page translates and the key comes from your own project.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Payment Processing
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Choose who takes card payments. You can use more than one.

- [Stripe](https://stripe.com/): cards, Apple Pay and Google Pay; you handle sales tax. Keys: [Stripe API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys).
- [PayPal](https://www.paypal.com/business): customers who prefer PayPal. Keys: [developer dashboard](https://developer.paypal.com/dashboard/).
- [Paddle](https://www.paddle.com/) or [Polar](https://polar.sh/): a merchant of record, who handles sales tax and VAT for you, for a higher fee ([Paddle pricing](https://www.paddle.com/pricing), [Polar docs](https://docs.polar.sh/)).

1. Open a business account and complete its identity checks.
2. Connect it in the plugin that takes the payments (such as Ultimate Multisite → Settings → Payments, or Fluent Forms → Payments), in test mode first. Keys go in that plugin's settings, never in a task.
3. Make a test purchase end to end, then switch to live mode.

Done when a live payment reaches your account and its receipt email arrives.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Backups, Updates and Uptime Alerts
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Keeps the site safe to change and tells you when it is down, before your customers do. The steps are for Hostinger; other hosts have the same three things under other names.

1. **Backups.** In hPanel, open the website's **Backups** ([guide](https://docs.hostinger.com/websites/backups)) and check recent backups are listed. Premium plans back up weekly, Business and Cloud plans daily (or add **Daily backups**). A site that takes orders, bookings or messages needs daily. Email mailboxes are not in website backups.
2. **Before a big change** (updating by hand, an import, a new plugin), click **Generate backup** first (once a day at most) and wait until it shows in the list. Entry-level plans need Business or higher for this; until then, download the latest automatic backup instead. Once, **Download** a backup and check it holds the site's files and its database (`.sql`) file, so you know it is usable. Never test **Restore** on the live site: it overwrites the current files and database. To try changes first, use a [staging copy](https://docs.hostinger.com/wordpress/staging) where the plan includes it (not on WordPress multisite).
3. **Updates: choose one updater**, so two never compete. In hPanel, open the WordPress site's **Security** page ([guide](https://docs.hostinger.com/wordpress/security)). **Smart auto-updates** lets Hostinger update WordPress, plugins and themes at the level you choose (keep at least security updates on; [what it changes](https://docs.hostinger.com/wordpress/hostinger-plugins/must-use-plugins/smart-auto-updates)). **Native auto-updates** leaves it to WordPress (Plugins → Enable auto-updates, per plugin). Premium plugins and themes update from their own servers with their licence or updater.
4. **Once a month**, open Dashboard → Updates (or ask your AI for `wp plugin list --update=available`), take a backup, install what is waiting, then check the home page, a form and wp-admin. Add a card for anything that broke.
5. **Uptime alert.** On Hostinger Agency Hosting, open hPanel → **Websites → Monitoring** ([guide](https://docs.hostinger.com/websites/monitoring)) and create an alert for the site's address, sent to the support mailbox. On other plans (Cloud, Business and others do not have this menu), follow **Setup Uptime Monitoring (updown.io)**, the next task, which also gives the site a public status page. Write which one you used in a comment here.

Done when a backup within the site's interval is listed (the last day for a site that needs daily, otherwise the last week), one downloaded backup has been checked, a comment here names the updater chosen and who checks updates each month, and the uptime alert is saved.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Uptime Monitoring (updown.io)
fluentboards_tasks.after: Setup Backups, Updates and Uptime Alerts
fluentboards_tasks.description:
[updown.io](https://updown.io/r/kddkt) checks the site from several countries and emails you when it stops answering, its SSL certificate is about to expire, or it gets slow, and gives it a public status page with its uptime and response times. It is pay-as-you-go: each check request uses one credit, so a check every 5 minutes uses about 8,640 credits a month. Skip this task if the site already has an uptime monitor you are happy with.

1. **Account.** Add the check to the [updown.io](https://updown.io/r/kddkt) account that already monitors your other sites: one account covers them all, and each site still gets its own status page. Sign up with the support mailbox's address only when there is no account yet, so alerts reach whoever looks after the site.
2. **Check.** Click **Add a check**, enter the home page's full address (`https://` and the address visitors use, after any redirect) and choose the interval: 5 minutes suits most sites, 1 minute a site that takes orders or bookings. In the check's options, set the text the page must contain to something the home page always shows (such as the site's name in the footer), so an error page that still answers counts as down.
3. **Alerts.** In updown.io's alert settings add the support mailbox (and, if you like, a phone for SMS or a chat app), and select it for the check. Wait for the first green result.
4. **Status page.** Give the site a status page on its own subdomain, `status.` plus the site's domain. In updown.io create a status page and add the site's check, then open the page's **Setup a custom domain** link: it lists two DNS records and has nothing to fill in, because the records alone put the page on the address. Add both at the DNS host: name `status`, type `CNAME`, target `page.updown.io`; and name `_updown.status`, type `TXT`, value `updown-page=p/` followed by the page's code, exactly as that screen shows it. For a site on a subdomain such as `shop.example.com`, the names in the `example.com` zone are `status.shop` and `_updown.status.shop` (in a zone of its own for `shop.example.com`, just `status` and `_updown.status`). In Cloudflare set Proxy status to **DNS only**; if the record must stay proxied, add two CAA records on that name, `0 issue "letsencrypt.org"` and `0 issue "sectigo.com"`, and do not use Flexible TLS, which loops. A site on a subdomain needs DNS only, because Cloudflare's free certificate covers one level. On a multisite network with sites at subdomains, keep the `*` wildcard record: the `status` record takes precedence, so no site may be called `status`. updown.io issues the page's certificate on the first visit after the records resolve, so the first try can show a certificate error: open the address again a minute later. Without access to the DNS, make the check public instead: its page (`https://updown.io/` and the check's code) shows visitors the uptime and response times.
5. **Website status link (optional).** To link the status page from the site, add a link to `#website-status` (for example the text **Website status** in the footer), then in SEO Pro Stack → Links switch on **Website status link** and paste the `https://status.` address. While it is off, links to `#website-status` are left out, so a theme can ship the link and each site decides whether to show it. Or ask your AI for `wp seoprostack status-link set <address> --on`.

Done when the check shows the site up, the support mailbox is selected for its alerts, the `https://status.` address loads with a valid certificate and shows the check, and a comment here gives that address and whether the site links to it.

**With aidevops:** your AI can create the check and status page with `updown-helper.sh`, add both DNS records through the DNS host's API and check them with `updown-helper.sh status-page domain`; no updown.io screen is needed.

fluentboards_tasks.title: Setup Project Management (Fluent Boards)
fluentboards_tasks.description:
Project Management is switched on for this site. Fluent Boards keeps work in boards: a board is a list of tasks in columns (stages) such as To-Do, In Progress and Done, and you move each task along as it is worked on. Use one board per area of work, such as the website, a client or a campaign.

1. In WordPress, open **Fluent Boards** and click **Add Board** (or the plus button).
2. Give it a name and a short description, choose **To-Do board**, and click **Create**. Boards already here, such as **Website** and **Website Setup**, came with the site: look at them first, to see how a board reads.
3. Open the board, click **Add a stage** and name the steps your work goes through (for example To-Do, In Progress, Done). Put a final stage that means finished at the end, so closed work leaves your sight.
4. Add the first task: click **Add Task** in the first stage, give it a clear name saying what done looks like, then open it to add a description, a due date and a label.
5. Add people: open the board's menu, choose **Members** and add each person by their WordPress account. Open a task to assign it, so each task has one person who owns it.
6. Ask people to switch on notifications in Fluent Boards, so they hear about tasks assigned to them and comments, without checking the board.

Done when the board has its stages, its members and at least one task assigned to someone. Never put a password or key in a task or comment.
